newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Thousands defy police threat in Belgrade demo.
newsitem.headline: Thousands defy police threat in Belgrade demo.

text.p: Thousands of students led by girls carrying flowers demonstrated against Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic in Belgrade on Monday in defiance of a government threat to crack down on two weeks of street unrest.
As a snowstorm blanketed the capital, eyewitnesses estimated more than 10,000 students joined the start of a protest march that was expected to gather support as it progressed.

"They teach us to think for ourselves here at universities but now Slobo and his mates expect us to switch off our brains when they speak," a philosophy student said. "Only a five-year-old would be fooled by this."
The size of the turnout indicated that a warning from the socialist government on Sunday that police were running out of patience with daily demonstrations had failed to cool dissent.
The police presence was unobtrusive in spite of the threat to confront the marchers but the socialist authorities have mobilised large reserves of security forces in readiness.

The protests, attracting up to 100,000 people a day in Belgrade, began against alleged rigging by the ruling socialists of municipal elections won by the Zajedno (Together) coalition of opposition parties.
Demonstrators are now demanding Milosevic's overthrow in the longest sustained challenge he has faced in nine years of power.

Vuk Draskovic, a leader of Zajedno, said the threat to unleash the police showed that "Mr Milosevic is in a state of panic. He made this statement ... to try to prevent people demonstrating today. But he will not succeed. We are not cowards."
Student organisers vowed not to be intimidated and said in a statement:

"The authorities claim we are just a few manipulated students and provocateurs. What serious state would put on alert the repressive machinery of 100,000 police against a small group of young rebels?"
Milosevic has publicly ignored the protests and held back his police in contrast with tough measures to quell previous unrest against his rule.
He used tanks to smash demonstrations in 1991 and riot police have been deployed quickly in the past at any whiff of trouble.
Zoran Djindjic, another Zajedno leader, forecast that the government warning would provoke more people into joining the protest marches and rallies in the centre of Belgrade.
The opposition wants to spread the protests to other parts of the country in an effort to bring Milosevic down.
Djindjic said strikes in industrial centres may be launched soon and added: "We shall bring the political crisis to boiling point."
Zajedno marches have been mainly peaceful except for a few days in which protesters threw stones at the state television and state newspaper offices, shattering windows.
Opposition stewards have stopped the stone-throwing since Thursday and demonstrators since then have hurled eggs at the two buildings -- symbols of Milosevic's authoritarian rule.
The speaker of parliament from the ruling socialist party, Dragan Tomic, branded the opposition "fascist".
Milosevic's socialists have already cracked down on independent news media. Radio B-92's signal has been jammed and journalists at state papers have complained of censorship.
Zajedno leaders said they planned to stage a boycott of parliament on Tuesday unless it annuls the results of the local elections.
